documents.title: Hog Trial
documents.text: Hog Trial In 1873 Randolph McCoy accused Floyd Hatfield of stealing his hog. A trial followed, presided over by Reverend Anderson Hatfield, justice of the peace. To be fair, the jury consisted of six Hatfields and six McCoys. One witness, William Staton, stated he had seen Floyd mark the hog's ear. This resulted in Floyd's acquittal. Presented by Pikeville-Pike County Tourism. (Reverse) Election Fight - In August 1882 an election was held near Jerry Hatfield's house. A fight broke out between Tolbert McCoy and Elias Hatfield. documents.title: McCoy Cemetery
documents.text: McCoy Cemetery Among the graves in the McCoy Cemetery are those of Randolph McCoy's three sons -Tolbert, Pharmer, and Randolph Jr.-all killed by the Hatfields. Also buried here are Alifair and Calvin McCoy, who were killed by the Hatfields when cabin was burned. Cemetery is part of the Hatfield-McCoy Feud Historic District. Presented by Pikeville-Pike County Tourism. Dedicated June 10, 2001. Pike 4087 US Highway 319, Hardy, KY 41531 (N 37 36.188, W 082 12.925) Markers

documents.title: William Ramey
documents.text: William Ramey William Ramey, born ca. 1782, came from North Carolina. He purchased 200-acre tract near the mouth of Elkhorn Creek in 1816. Served as justice of the peace, sheriff, and commissioner of roads in Pike Co. Acquired thousands of acres by land surveys and county court orders. The founder of Elkhorn City, his descendants still live in the area. Presented by Elkhorn City Area Heritage Council and Descendants of William Ramey. Dedicated September 1, 2001. Pike Elkhorn City, Patty Loveless and Russell Streets, KY 80 & 197 Markers

documents.title: Elkhorn City's Railroads
documents.text: Elkhorn City's Railroads Two major railroads, C & O from north and Clinchfield from south, connected at Elkhorn City, Feb. 8, 1915, opening up trade from Ohio Valley to South Atlantic Region. Elkhorn City became important railroad town. Trains went through several times a day transporting goods from north and south and coal and timber from surrounding area. Presented by Elkhorn City Heritage Council, Inc. Dedicated March 27, 2004. Pike Pine St., Elkhorn City Markers

documents.title: Richard Potter
documents.text: Richard Potter One of the first pioneers to settle in Breaks Canyon area, Richard married Mary Ramey in 1821 and had 11 children; later married Mary "Polly" Wallace. He was a farmer, hunter, and a distillery operator. Richard acquired several thousand acres of land including present-day Breaks Interstate Park and Carson Island, formerly Potter Plantation. Presented by Elkhorn City Heritage Council, Inc. Dedicated March 27, 2004. Pike Elkhorn City, Patty Loveless Dr., KY 80 Markers

documents.text: McCoy House After Hatfields burned the McCoy home, January 1, 1888, Randolph and Sarah McCoy never returned to Blackberry Creek. Governors of Ky. and West Va. urged Hatfields and McCoys to move away from each other. McCoys purchased house near river bank on East Main St., and Randolph operated a ferry across the Big Sandy River. Dedicated June 10, 2004 Pike Pikeville, 235 Main Street Markers

documents.title: Sally McCoy
documents.text: Sally McCoy Sarah Elizabeth (Sally) McCoy was the daughter of Roseanna McCoy and Johnse Hatfield. Her parents' love affair played a role in the infamous Hatfield-McCoy feud. Although circumstances prohibited the two from marrying, the child was born in 1881 and lived with her mother and Aunt Betty McCoy. (Reverse) Sally McCoy contracted measles and pneumonia, and died a few months after her birth. The death of Roseanna McCoy's only child, Sally, was a contributing factor in the grief and sorrow that led to the untimely death of Roseanna. Sally was laid to rest in the cemetery at top of hill. Grave is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Dedicated June 10, 2005 Pike Ky. Hwy. 29

documents.title: Daniel Boone's First Steps in Kentucky
documents.text: Daniel Boone's First Steps in Kentucky Boone 1st visited Ky. on hunting trip in 1767-68. Hunted Clinch River before coming to Russell Fork of the Big Sandy River. Followed rim of Breaks Canyon through present-day Elkhorn City. He tracked 50 miles along buffalo trace to a salt lick at modern David, Ky. Wintered there before following same route home. Dedicated May 27, 2006. Pike KY 80, Elkhorn City Markers

documents.title: John Paul Riddle, 1901-1989
documents.text: John Paul Riddle, 1901-1989 Aviation pioneer graduated from Pikeville College Academy in 1920. Flew plane under Pikeville’s Middle Bridge on July 4, 1923. Trained as a pilot in U.S. Army, he & T. Higbee Embry founded the Embry-Riddle Flying School in Cincinnati, 1925. Incorporated four years later as part of AVCO, which later became American Airlines. Over Founded the Embry-Riddle School of Aviation in Miami, Fla. During WWII, trained pilots for U.S. and Britain. Later became Embry-Riddle Aeronautical Univ. Inducted into the Ky. Aviation Hall of Fame and Fla. Aviation Historical Society. Received British Empire award and honorary degrees from Pikeville College & E-R Aeronautical Univ. Dedica

documents.title: John May (1760-1813)
documents.text: John May (1760-1813) Born in Lancaster, Pa. to immigrant German parents. Joined 4th Virginia Infantry in fall of 1776. Saw Geo. Washington’s retreat across the Hudson in Nov. Served until 1779. Married Sarah Phillips in 1780. Settled in Shelby Valley in 1800. Sarah swore to a declaration for a widow’s Rev. War pension in Pike Co. Court in 1845. (Reverse) John May Family- Three sons stayed in E. Kentucky: Samuel in Prestonsburg served in the Ky. House and Senate in the 1830s; Thomas built a state road from Pikeville into Shelby Valley, was JP and sheriff of Pike Co.; Reuben’s farm became Maytown on Beaver Cr. documents.title: Liberty First County Seat
documents.text: Liberty First County Seat Kentucky legislature established Pike County Dec. 19, 1821. First county seat was located near here on the Peyton Justice farm and named Liberty. No courthouse was built here due to opposition to site. On Dec. 24, 1823, new county seat selected at Peach Orchard Bottom, Pikeville, on property of Elijah Adkins, where it is today. Presented by Pike County Fiscal Court. Dedicated August 8, 2013. Pike 4127 E.Shelbiana Rd., Pikeville Markers

documents.title: Frank and Nancy McCoy Phillips
documents.text: Frank and Nancy McCoy Phillips Frank Phillips was instrumental in the capture of the Hatfield family and allies involved in the 1882 shooting death of three McCoy brothers. In 1888 Governor Buckner appointed Phillips, former deputy sheriff, as special envoy to arrest indicted Hatfields hiding in W.Va. He later left law enforcement to raise a family. He died at age 36. (Reverse) Nancy McCoy was the youngest daughter of Asa Harmon McCoy, the first man killed in Hatfield-McCoy Feud. Despite the feud, at age 15 she married Johnse Hatfield, son of Anderson Hatfield. documents.title: Col. John Dils, Jr.
documents.text: Col. John Dils, Jr. Born in Parkersburg, WV, in 1818, Dils came to Pikeville ca. 1840 and became a merchant. In Oct. 1861, while the area was under Confederate control, he was arrested for Union sympathies. Sent to Libby Prison in Richmond, VA, he was quickly released. In Feb. 1862, he went to Washington, D.C. to meet with President Lincoln. Over. Upon returning to E. Ky., he raised a regiment that became the 39th Ky. Mounted Inf. (Union), which fought several large engagements in this region during Civil War. Dismissed from the service in 1863, Dils later helped bring education and industry to this area. documents.title: Early Iron Works
documents.text: Early Iron Works Though there is evidence of iron production in area even earlier, land was bought for this purpose, 1805, by Robert Clark Jr. and Wm. Smith. Known as Clark & Smith's Iron Works, 1805-1808. A blast furnace called Red River Iron Works operated here from 1808 to 1830. Rebuilt as Estill Steam Furnace on another site; closed in 1869. (Reverse) Clay City Timber Industry - With Kentucky Union Railway Company's track laid in Powell Co. in 1886, the area's timber industry expanded. Red River Lumber Mills (1880) became largest steampowered sawmill in Ky. In 1890, the steady run began at one of America's largest timber processing plants. documents.title: Morgan's First Raid
documents.text: Morgan's First Raid CSA General John H. Morgan's first Kentucky raid covered 1,000 miles, July 4 to July 28, 1862-24 days. Left Tenn. with 900 men, returned with 1200, captured 17 towns, 300 horses, destroyed Union supplies. Here, July 21, Morgan took over telegraph line and countermanded USA orders to pursue. Destroyed commissary stores, wagons, arms. Moved on to Monticello. See map. Pulaski Somerset, Library lawn Markers

documents.title: Dutton's Hill Battle
documents.text: Dutton's Hill Battle March 30, 1863, USA force of 1,250 under General Q. A. Gillmore overtook 1,550 Confederate cavalry under Gen. John Pegram, here. Five-hour battle resulted. CSA driven from one position to another, withdrew during night across Cumberland. Killed, wounded, missing, CSA 200 and USA 30. On nine-day expedition into Ky., CSA had captured 750 cattle and took 537 across river. Pulaski 2 mi. N. of Somerset, KY 39 Markers

documents.title: Confederate Defense Line
documents.text: Confederate Defense Line Late in 1861, Confederates sought to prevent Union forces from occupying strategic points in Kentucky and Tennessee, to maintain rail shipments of vital Confederate supplies from Virginia south and west, and to set up bases for future offensive thru Kentucky and Ohio to divide eastern and western Union states. With those aims the Confederate Defense Line was formed from the Big Sandy Valley in east Kentucky thru Cumberland Gap, Mill Springs on Cumberland River, Bowling Green on L & N Ry., to Columbus, Ky. on the Mississippi River. documents.title: Burnside
documents.text: Burnside First named Point Isabel. Settled about 1800 by pioneers from the Carolinas and Virginia. During the Civil War the Union army, in 1863, set up a troop rendezvous and supply base here as a prelude to East Tennessee campaign of Gen. Ambrose E. Burnside. The area became known as Camp Burnside in official dispatches and the name Burnside retained after war. Pulaski 8801 S. Hwy. 27, Burnside Markers

documents.title: Town Spring
documents.text: Town Spring Near the site of this spring Somerset was established as the county seat in 1801 on forty acres given by William Dodson. The path to it became the town's most traveled street in order to drink from the Old Town Spring. Thus a saying became popular, "Whoever drinks from the Old Town Spring will have wisdom and will always return to Somerset." Over. (Reverse) Pulaski County, 1799 As Kentucky's 27th county, its territory was taken from Lincoln and Green counties and named for Count Casimir Pulaski, a Polish patriot and soldier, who came to America when he learned of the Colonies' fight for freedom. documents.title: Home of Governor Morrow
documents.text: Home of Governor Morrow Edwin P. Morrow (1877-1935), a native of Somerset, built this house soon after marrying in 1903; he began his Somerset law practice same year. Morrow served in Spanish-American War; appointed U.S. District Attorney for eastern Kentucky by Pres. Taft and elected governor in 1919. A popular orator, he was nephew of Governor Wm. O. Bradley. Buried in Frankfort Cem. Pulaski 208 East Oak St., Somerset Markers

documents.text: Harriette Simpson Arnow (1908-1986) The author of such celebrated Appalachian novels as The Dollmaker and Hunter's Horn; social histories include Seedtime on the Cumberland and Flowering of the Cumberland. Born in Wayne County, Arnow spent most of her childhood in Burnside. Moved to Michigan during World War II, but continued to chronicle Appalachian life and people. Pulaski Burnside, US 27 Markers

documents.title: Felix K. Zollicoffer
documents.text: Felix K. Zollicoffer Brig. Gen. Felix K. Zollicoffer, CSA, died here, Jan. 19, 1862, in Battle of Logan's Crossroads (Mill Springs). This Tenn. native was veteran of Seminole War, editor of Nashville Banner, and 3-term U.S. congressman. In heavy rain and smoke of battle, Zollicoffer was killed approaching USA lines, which he mistook for own troops. Over. Presented by Boy Scout Troop 79 of Somerset for the Kentucky Bicentennial. (Reverse) "Zollie Tree" - This large, white oak has been decorated annually in honor of Gen. Zollicoffer since 1902, when Dorotha Burton began tradition. Over 100 CSA soldiers are in mass grave at rear of park. Zollicoffer is buried in Nashville. Boy Scout Troop 79 Tr

documents.title: Beech Grove/Noble Ellis
documents.text: Beech Grove/Noble Ellis In late 1861, Confederate Gen. Felix Zollicoffer advanced into Ky. from Jamestown, Tn. Zollicoffer ordered seizure of area ferry boats to cross his army to the north side of the Cumberland River. Unable to locate adequate boats, Zollicoffer constructed transports at Mill Springs. On December 5, 1861, he crossed his army and built a winter camp here at Beech Grove. (Reverse) Noble Ellis- At Beech Grove, Zollicoffer’s army was supplied by a steamboat, the Noble Ellis. When the Confederates were defeated at the Battle of Mill Springs on Jan. 19, 1862, they returned to their camp here. documents.title: Boone Way
documents.text: Boone Way The 96-mile stretch of road from Crab Orchard to Cumberland Gap was known as the Boone Way. Colonel James Maret, an early advocate of road improvement, was responsible for cutting of roadbed and its first paving. As L & N railroad agent and telegraph operator in Mt. Vernon, Maret developed a concern for road conditions. Highway was in use by 1918; the Boone Way became US 25. (Reverse) Col. James Maret (1855-1936) - Born in Garrard Co., Maret came here in 1877. He established this county's first telephone exchange and newspaper; was town clerk for 25 years. documents.text: Morgan Raiders' Camp On last tragic raid, the fourth into Kentucky, Morgan's Raiders took Mt. Sterling, then lost it, took Lexington and June 11, 1864 took Cynthiana. documents.title: Moonlight Schools
documents.text: Moonlight Schools Established in Rowan County, Ky., in 1911, by Mrs. Cora W. Stewart, "to emancipate from illiteracy those enslaved in its bondage." Because the people had to labor by day it was decided to have the schools on moonlight nights so the moon could light the way. The schools were taught by volunteer teachers. Movement soon spread nationally and internationally. Rowan Morehead, Wilkinson Blvd., US 60 Markers

documents.title: Rowan County "War," 1884-1887
documents.text: Rowan County "War," 1884-1887 Political tensions led to this three-year period of violence which resulted in some twenty deaths. Conflict between John Martin and Floyd Tolliver caused Tolliver's death. His brother Craig opposed Martin ally D.B. Logan and killed two of Logan's cousins. Tolliver group then seized virtual control of the county. See over. Presented by Rowan County Fiscal Court. documents.text: Jamestown Skirmishes Dec. 25, 1861, part of First Ky. Cav., USA, camped at Webb's Cross Roads to guard stored corn and forage and scout CSA operations. Detachment skirmished with enemy here resulting in one death, CSA. Both armies in area again, 1863. On June 2, 300 CSA attacked Union pickets, driving them into town. CSA retired when met by alert USA. One CSA man and weapons captured. Russell Jamestown, US 127 Markers

documents.title: Chalybeate Springs
documents.text: Chalybeate Springs A health resort long known as Big Boiling Springs, operated before 1850 by family of Sam Patterson, among the earliest settlers. Log cabins (12) called Long Row were built for guests who came here for amusement, pleasure, and the medicinal iron and sulphur water. In 1898, large hotel built which burned in 1942. The spring has been capped for use as a well. Russell Russell Springs, Corner Jamestown & Main Sts. Markers

documents.title: Forage Depot-Civil War
documents.text: Forage Depot-Civil War In Dec. 1861, Col. Frank Wolford, USA, with Companies A, B, C and H left Camp Billy Williams enroute to Webbs Cross Roads. Here they guarded forage collected and stored by Lieutenant Silas Adams, Regimental Quartermaster of First Ky. Cavalry. July 4, 1862, the First Ky. Cavalry bivouacked here one night; next day Col. Wolford marched with them on to Lebanon. Russell Poplar Grove Church, US 127 Markers

documents.title: Remember the Raisin
documents.text: Remember the Raisin Rendezvous of Kentucky Volunteers, Aug. 15, 1812, ordered to relieve Gen. Hull at Detroit. Kentuckians took Frenchtown (Monroe) on Raisin River Jan. 18, 1813. Four days later enemy attacked-killed, massacred, wounded, or captured all but 30. Of 1050 men not half reached home. Ky. counties named for officers: Allen, Ballard, Graves, Hart, Hickman, Edmonson, McCracken, Meade, Simpson. Dedicated August 5, 1962. For more information, see ExploreKYHistory: Remember the Raisin! documents.text: Confederate Governor Home of George W. Johnson, born 1811 in Scott Co. Named first Confederate Governor of Ky. in Nov. 1861, he followed CSA army's withdrawal to Tenn. from Bowling Green in Feb., 1862. He became aide to General John C. Breckinridge but fought as private in Battle of Shiloh and mortally wounded, Apr. 7, 1862 - still as CSA Governor. Burial was in cemetery here. Originally installed on June 22, 1964. documents.title: Georgetown Raided
documents.text: Georgetown Raided CSA Gen. John H. Morgan, on Kentucky raid here, July 15, 1862, camped two days. Destroyed rail bridges, USA stores, dispersed Home Guards. On 17th defeated USA at Cynthiana. Started back to Tenn. On last raid, Morgan was here, July 10, 1864, after taking Lexington. On 12th CSA met defeat at Cynthiana and retreated to Virginia. documents.text: Cardome Home of Gov. James F. Robinson, 1844 until death, at age 82, in 1882. documents.title: Hemp in Scott County
documents.text: Hemp in Scott County Rev. Elijah Craig established at Georgetown, in 1789, one of the earliest ropewalks, which were long sheds for spiral winding of hemp fibers. Also started fulling mill in 1793. Both factories made cordage and rigging for vessels built on the Ohio and Kentucky Rivers. Peak production in 1839; over 1,000 tons processed yearly with value of $120,000. See over. (Reverse) Hemp in Kentcky - First crop grown, 1775. From 1840 to 1860, Ky.'s production largest in U.S. Peak in 1850 was 40,000 tons, with value of $5,000,000. Scores of factories made twine, rope, gunny sacks, bags for cotton picking and marketing. documents.title: Scott County, 1792
documents.text: Scott County, 1792 Formed out of a part of Woodford County, it was the second created after Kentucky became a state. Named for Gen. Charles Scott, 1739-1813, a Va. native. Officer in Revolution, saw service at Trenton, 1776, Germantown and Monmouth, 1777, Stony Point, 1779. Came to Kentucky in 1785. Represented Woodford Co. in the Va. Assembly, 1789-90. Fourth governor of Ky., 1808-12. Scott Georgetown, Courthouse lawn, US 25, 460 Markers

documents.text: Patriot's Stage Stop This house, 1800-32, a stagecoach stop owned by Julius Gibbs. On the Iron Works Pike, route for hauling iron products from furnaces in Bath County to Kentucky River. Gibbs enlisted 1775, in first Va. Regiment under Col. Patrick Henry. Served until 1781. Pioneer settler of Great Crossings, 1782. Charter member of its Baptist church, 1785. Presented by Mrs. Lena Gibbs Ransdell and Gibbs' Descendants. Designed by Thomas Boyd of Pittsburgh, who served as supervising architect. (Reverse) Goebel Trial Here - Scott County courthouse chosen by Judge J. E. Parish, second oldest in the state, was formed by Maryland settlers who arrived in 1786. First church built circa 1794; resident pastor was Reverend Stephen Theodore Badin, first priest ordained in U.S. Present church constructed in 1820 at a cost of $3,600. Formed when bison herds trampled the soil by the spring, the area was at the junction of several trails used by migrating herds. After the bison left, the spring served the area's human inhabitants who settled the town of Herndonsville (later Stamping Ground) in the early 1800s. documents.title: Historic Stamping Ground Jail
documents.text: Historic Stamping Ground Jail OLD STAMPING GROUND JAIL Built ca. 1890, the brick, two-cell jail was used until the 1970s. The building survived three historic disasters. In 1916 and 1925, two intense fires destroyed most city buildings. On April 3, 1974, a tornado leveled more than 300 homes and buildings in Stamping Ground, yet the jail remained standing. OLD STAMPING GROUND JAIL While it operated, many inmates maintained city streets to pay off fines. On September 18, 1899, Stamping Ground made national headlines when Town Marshal Charles Richard Duke was killed in the line of duty. documents.text: The Blockhouse Built in 1858 by townspeople for civil defense against guerrillas. Located in middle of intersection. Measured 12 by 18 feet with loopholes on all sides. Manned by townsmen when alarm sounded. Several encounters with gangs attempting to raid town. Torn down in 1870 when civil law and order were assured, and marauders had been dispersed. John Simpson Simpsonville and Simpson County, Kentucky, were named for the Captain who fought with Wayne at Fallen Timbers, practiced law in Shelbyville, and was elected to the State Legislature four times. documents.title: The Armstrong Hotel
documents.text: The Armstrong Hotel Established in 1859 by George A. Armstrong and was known for its good food and lodgings. Guerrilla leader Ed Terrell stopped here briefly, May 26, 1866. Attempting to escape, he was mortally wounded nearby. Brig. Gen. Henry H. Denhardt was slain here, Sept. 20, 1937. When the hotel was destroyed by fire on February 7, 1944, the owners decided not to rebuild. Shelby 6th & Main Sts., Shelbyville Markers

documents.title: Shelby County, 1792
documents.text: Shelby County, 1792 Formed from a part of Jefferson County, it was the third created after Kentucky became a state. Named in honor of Isaac Shelby, 1750-1826, first Kentucky governor, 1792-96; elected again 1812-16. In the Revolutionary War, Indian campaigns, and War of 1812. He came to Kentucky in 1783. Member of the Kentucky Constitutional Conventions at Danville, 1784-92. Shelby Courthouse lawn, 5th & Main Sts., Shelbyville Markers

documents.title: Shelby County Hemp
documents.text: Shelby County Hemp One of chief producing counties. Crop income reached a yearly high of $150,000 in 1860. Nine hundred tons of hemp were consumed to produce 2,000 bales of twine and 5,000 coils of rope this same year. One of the ten Bluegrass counties which accounted for more than 90 percent of the yield of the whole country in the late 1800s. (Reverse) Hemp in Kentucky - First crop grown, 1775. From 1840 to 1860, Ky.'s production largest in U.S. Peak in 1850 was 40,000 tons, with value of $5,000,000. Scores of factories made twine, rope, oakum to caulk sailing ships and cotton bagging. documents.text: Thelma Stovall (1919-1994) Entered political service in 1949 when she was elected to the Kentucky state legislature. documents.title: Lewis and Clark in Kentucky- Death of Meriwether Lewis
documents.text: Lewis and Clark in Kentucky- Death of Meriwether Lewis William Clark, coleader of the famous Lewis and Clark Expedition to the Pacific, spent the night of October 28, 1809, at John Shannon's Tavern near present Graefenburg. That day he read that Lewis, his expedition partner, had killed himself in Tenn. Over. (Reverse) That night Clark wrote a famous letter expressing fear that Lewis had committed suicide. He wrote, "I fear O! I fear the weight of his mind has overcome him." Lewis died Oct. 11, 1809, 70 mi. sw of Nashville on the Natchez Trace. Dedicated October 1, 2006. Shelby US 60 & KY 1472 near Graefenburg Markers

documents.title: Horrible Massacre
documents.text: Horrible Massacre On January 25, 1865, Co. E. 5th United States Colored Calvary (USCC) attacked by Confederate guerillas while driving herd of 900 cattle to Louisville. About 22 men killed and at least eight severely wounded. Based at Camp Nelson, nearly all of the recruits were former slaves. The 5th also fought in 1864 Saltville battles. (Reverse) African American Cemetery- The 5th USCC troopers killed in 1865 Simpsonville slaughter were buried in a mass grave by local residents. Area used as African American cemetery. documents.title: Octagon Hall
documents.text: Octagon Hall An antebellum landmark built by Andrew Jackson Caldwell, an ardent advocate of the southern cause. Many Confederate soldiers found shelter here. Bricks were made, wood cut and finished, stone quarried on the place. The house erected by Caldwell and his men. Three floors, with four large rooms, hall and stairway. Large basement provided hiding place. Dedicated in August 1962. For more information, see ExploreKYHistory: Octagon Hall Simpson N. of Franklin, US 31-W Markers

documents.title: Sue Mundy's" Grave
documents.text: Sue Mundy's" Grave Marcellus Jerome Clarke enlisted in the Confederate Army, 1861, at age 17. Attached to Morgan's Cavalry in 1863. Captured on March 12, 1865, taken to Louisville, hanged three days later, court-martialed as guerrilla "Sue Mundy." His last words: "I believe in and die for the Confederate cause." In 1865 body brought here, reburied 1914 two blocks east by CSA veterans. Dedicated February 8, 1963. documents.text: Lincoln School A hallmark of the black community, it was dedicated on September 8, 1940 and G. R. Houston served as its first principal. In 1944, county schools merged with Lincoln, which brought about crowded conditions. School added onto several times from 1955 to 1961. It served the Harristown district until schools were integrated in 1965. (Reverse) The school theme was “so teach us, that we may apply our hearts to wisdom.” Colors were purple and gold. School was the focus for community activities and a great source of pride for a quarter of a century. documents.text: Alexander Majors Cofounder of the Pony Express, he was born near this site on Oct. 4, 1814. Five years later, his family moved to Mo. Territory. In 1849, he formed a freighting business from Mo. to Santa Fe. In 1854, became partners with Wm. Russell and Wm. Waddell hauling military & civilian freight. By 1859, had 3500 wagons, 40,000 oxen, 4000 men, 1000 mules. Presented by the Simpson Co. Historical Society (Reverse) Started the Pony Express in 1860. Mail was carried on horseback from Mo. to Ca. in 10 days. Ended when overland telegraph completed, 1861. William “Buffalo Bill” Cody, who had worked for Majors as a youth, found him writing memoirs. documents.title: James Morrison Heady (1829-1915)
documents.text: James Morrison Heady (1829-1915) The Blind Bard of Kentucky was blind by fifteen and deaf before forty. Neither condition limited his contributions. As friends read aloud, he embossed notes on the Diplograph machine he invented and built. He invented the Talking Glove with the alphabet printed on it so others could communicate by touching the letters. (Reverse) Heady’s other inventions included the pull-chain home farm gate, furniture, utensils, and games. Built a steam-powered embossing press for American Printing House for the Blind, and wrote and published prose, poetry, and songs. Entombed with his parents in the Elk Creek Cemetery. Dedicated July 17, 2004. Spencer Elk Creek, at Cemetery

documents.text: Independence Day-1863 Morgan's Raiders, on way to Ohio, July 4, 1863, approached 200 USA Mich. Inf. under Col. O. H. Moore intrenched here. Morgan demanded surrender. Moore replied Fourth of July no day to entertain such a proposition. Eight CSA assaults repulsed in 3-hour battle, 36 CSA killed, 45 wounded. 6 USA killed, 23 wounded. Morgan bypassed and moved on after significant delay. Dedicated July 4, 1963. Taylor 9 mi. S. of Campbellsville, Bypass on old KY 55 Markers

documents.text: Confederate Raids General John Hunt Morgan's cavalry, returning from second Kentucky raid, here, Dec. 31, 1862. Took supplies. Went on to Tenn. On raid Union's rail supply line wrecked and $2,000,000 property destroyed. Morgan thru here again after three-hour battle at Tebb's Bend, July 4, 1863. Continued raid into Indiana to NE Ohio, where captured, July 26th. See map other side. Taylor Campbellsville, Courthouse lawn, US 68 Markers

documents.text: Campbellsville First settled about 1800. Town, established by Legislature, 1817, was made seat of government when county was formed. Established by Legislature, 1848, formed from a part of Green County. Named for Gen. Zachary Taylor, famed Kentucky soldier. Noted as Indian fighter: Ft. It was the trail traveled by the pioneers who came through the Cumberland Gap to settle the then new lands of Ky. and Tenn. Over. Andrew Jackson on his way to Washington, September 27, 1832. See over. (Reverse) Sanders Tavern - Henry Sanders, Jr., 1776-1844, settled in this county in 1795. Besides building Sanders Tavern, parts of which stood until about 1947, he also built "Clay Hill," the home of his son James Sanders. documents.text: Jefferson Davis' Salute to Kentucky "Kentucky, my own, my native land. God grant that peace and plenty may ever run throughout your borders. documents.text: First RFD in Kentucky First rural free delivery of mail in Kentucky was established at Allensville Post Office on Jan. 11, 1897. RFD enabled farmers to receive daily mail and avoid a drive to the post office. Two more Guthrie rallies in 1905-06. (Reverse) The Planters Protective Association advocated state & federal policies more responsive to farmers’ needs. documents.title: The Trenton School
documents.text: The Trenton School Trenton School was built in 1920 through the initiative of the citizens of Trenton, Kentucky. Funds were donated and the Board of Trustees personally borrowed the balance of the funds needed to complete construction of the school. Students from the first to the 12th grades were educated at the school. By 1935, the entire $42,000 debt was retired. In 1957, Trenton School merged with Todd County Schools and Trenton High School was closed. The school building continued as Trenton Elementary School until a county consolidation of all elementary schools in 1988. Trenton Community Center, Inc. purchased the school and gym in 1988 to preserve it for future generations of Trenton

documents.title: Richards Home Site
documents.text: Richards Home Site Lewis Richards, born Va., 1754. Sergeant with Gen. George Rogers Clark when he built first blockhouse at site of present Cincinnati. Went on, in attempt to save Kentuckians captured by English and Indians, 1779. Unable to overtake them, destroyed the Indian villages at Chillicothe and Piqua. Richards was a volunteer at battle of Blue Licks, 1782. Died here in 1846. Union E. of Boxville, KY 56 & 983 Markers

documents.title: The Robert E. Lee Won with Sturgis Coal
documents.text: The Robert E. Lee Won with Sturgis Coal Nearby coal fields supplied fuel to power steamboat Robert E. Lee in race against the Natchez , 1870. Greatest race in river history began in New Orleans and ended at St. Louis. Robert E. Lee won the championship of Mississippi River by 6 hours and 15 minutes. Both steamboat captains were natives of Kentucky. Union Sturgis, US 60 Markers

documents.title: Union County, 1811
documents.text: Union County, 1811 The 55th Kentucky county created, it was formed entirely out of Henderson County. "It was possibly so named because of the unanimity of its citizens for division of the old county." Morganfield made county seat. Named for Gen. Daniel Morgan, who owned the land. Officer throughout the Revolutionary War, from 1775 at Quebec to 1781 at Cowpens, S.C. Union Morganfield, Courthouse lawn, US 60, 641 Markers

documents.title: Lincoln Spoke Here
documents.text: Lincoln Spoke Here Abraham Lincoln's only political speech in his native state, here, 1840, at age 31. An elector from Illinois, he campaigned for Whig presidential candidate William Henry Harrison. From Shawneetown, across river, Lincoln led parade. Young ladies rode on floats drawn by white horses. Cannon for salute burst upon firing. Its breech is at Kentucky Historical Society. Union Morganfield, Courthouse lawn, KY 56 Markers

documents.title: Camp Breckinridge
documents.text: Camp Breckinridge Army post built in 1942, on 36,000 acres, at a cost of $39,000,000. Named for John C. Breckinridge, US Vice President, 1856-60; Confederate Secretary of War, 1865. Created as infantry training center for up to 40,000 men. Used during WW II, 1943-46, as prisoner of war camp for as many as 3,000 enlisted men of German Army. Camp deactivated in 1949. Over. (Reverse) Camp Breckinridge - During Korean War, 1950-54, camp reopened for training of infantry. From 1954 to 1963 used for summer training of 4,500 National Guard troops. documents.text: Morgan Springs Under the municipal building lies the old Morgan Springs, named for General Daniel Morgan of Revolutionary War fame. Water from spring furnishes a portion of the supply used by fountain in front of building. The city of Morganfield was established in 1811 on part of a military grant that was given to Daniel Morgan; Morganfield named for him. Union Main St. in front of City Hall, Morganfield, KY 56 Markers

documents.text: Nally Spa Four miles south of here stood the old Chalybeate Springs Resort Hotel featuring Sulphur Water Springs and a fresh water spring on its grounds from 1850 to 1890. The fresh water spring was renamed "Nally Spa" in 1975 to honor Union Countian James P. (Jimmy) Nally. Union Jct. KY 56 & 758 Markers

documents.title: St. Vincent's Academy
documents.text: St. Vincent's Academy Sisters of Charity from Nazareth-Angela Spink, Frances Gardner, and Cecily O'Brien-arrived here, 1820. They began a girls boarding school on this site on land of Alvey family. With aid of Father Elisha Durbin, school gained renown. It operated until 1967. First Catholic cemetery in county joins the school site. Buried here are several Revolutionary War soldiers. Union Between Waverly and Morganfield, near Jct. US 60 & KY 141 Markers

documents.title: Baseball Great
documents.text: Baseball Great Jackie Robinson (1919-1972) began his professional baseball career while a lieutenant at Camp Breckinridge, 1944. The next year Branch Rickey, Brooklyn Dodgers general manager, signed the four-sport letterman from UCLA for Montreal Royals, top Dodger farm club. In 1947, Robinson promoted to Dodgers team, breaking major league color barrier. Elected to Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962. Union 2-1/4 mi. from Morganfield at entrance to Earle C. Clements Job Corps Center, US 60 Markers

documents.title: George Huston
documents.text: George Huston A Harvard graduate and lawyer who specialized in land litigations, George Huston helped found city's first bank in 1869. He owned and enlarged this antebellum house from the early brick section where Dr. Brady, Huston's father-in-law, lived. At Civil War's end, Union soldiers camped here. In 1846 ex-President Tyler stayed here while Huston checked his land boundary. Union 205 N. Brady St., Morganfield Markers

documents.text: Earle C. Clements (1896-1985) This Union Countian became governor following service in World War I, then as sheriff, county clerk and judge, state senator. As governor, 1947-1950, Clements spurred massive industrialization effort as well as road and state parks development. Resigned to serve a term in U.S. Senate; ally of Lyndon Johnson. Later Ky. highway commissioner. documents.title: Bettie Taylor Phillips
documents.text: Bettie Taylor Phillips Born in Morganfield in 1830, she was one of several known as the “Mother of the Orphan Brigade.” Married W.S. Phillips in 1847. In 1861, accompanied him as he served in Gen. John C. Breckinridge’s 4th Ky. Inf., Co. C. She stayed with him throughout the war, providing aid and comfort to wounded and dying men. Over (Reverse) When returning home to Ky. due to illness, she was captured in Nashville and tried as a spy. After acquittal, she found her way back to the Brigade and was with CSA Pres. Davis and his wife just before their capture. She returned to Uniontown after war with the4th Infantry battle flag. Buried in Uniontown City Cemetery. Dedicated September 29, 2012.

documents.title: A Civil War Defense Line
documents.text: A Civil War Defense Line Troops under Generals S. B. Buckner and A. S. Johnston, CSA, took up this key position in the Southern defense line on September 18, 1861. After Fort Henry fell and Fort Donelson was threatened, they evacuated Feb. 11-13, 1862. Gen. O. M. Mitchell and Federal troops entered Feb. 14, 1862, occupying the evacuated fort and securing the defense line for the North. Warren Roland Bland Park, Bowling Green Markers

documents.text: Old Meeting House Green River Union Meeting House, part of Great Frontier Revival of early 1800's, and burial ground are three miles northwest. Huguenots came 1806 and 1814, organized and built log church, then about 1845 present meeting house. Methodists, Baptists, Presbyterians met there before building own churches in area. Many leading ministers of those days were trained there. Dedicated August 23, 1964. Old Stagecoach Stop (Marker Number: 1573) County: Warren Location: US 31-W, 8 mi. NE of Bowling Green Description: Built in 1841 by Samuel Murrell, this house was a well-known inn and stagecoach stop on Louisville-Nashville road until the L&N Railroad was completed in 1859. Led escape from Federal prison, Nov. '63. Leader of northwest conspiracy '64. Termed most dangerous man of Confederacy. Ky. Court of Appeals, 1878-98. Born Butler Co., 1838; lived here. documents.title: McFadin's Station
documents.text: McFadin's Station The first in this area, 1785. On north bank of Barren River, built by Andrew McFadin (McFadden), one of 8 brothers from N.C., all of whom fought in Revolutionary War. Five of them later came to Ky., settled along Barren River. Andrew made first surveys of much of the land in this region. McFadin's was stopover for Robert Moore, who founded Bowling Green about 1796. (Reverse) Cumberland Trace - McFadin's Station stood near the Cumberland Trace, an important artery in the development of this region, used by many who settled this area. documents.title: Civil War Occupations
documents.text: Civil War Occupations Threatened by Union forces to the west, CSA, who had occupied city five months and fortified hills, planned to evacuate Feb. 14, 1862. Other Federals came from north and bombarded from across the river. CSA set fire to depot and warehouses, as planned, night of 13th. Federals resumed bombardment next day, but ceased and entered city when informed CSA had gone. Warren Fountain Square, Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: Baker Hill
documents.text: Baker Hill One of nine hills fortified by CSA making Bowling Green a strong Confederate defense center, 1861. Feb. 14, 1862, day after CSA left the area, USA forces in command of Gen. Ormsby Mitchell bombarded the town from here. It continued until a civilian bearing flag of truce advised Federals CSA had gone. Residence on hilltop used as hospital by USA to end of war. Warren Old Louisville Rd., north of Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: College Hill
documents.text: College Hill Now known as Reservoir Hill, one of nine key fortifications of CSA defense during 1861 Civil War occupation of Bowling Green. Felled trees with sharpened ends were placed as cavalry barriers. Stones from a college building under construction went into the fortifications. The Bowling Green system was manned by approximately 4,000 Confederates. Warren Main & Park Sts., entrance to Reservoir Park, Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: Old Union Church
documents.text: Old Union Church Legislative Act of 1795 gave right to 200 acres for each settler in Green River country. This brought many from Carolinas. Among them were Baptists, two preachers, who constituted Union Church in 1795. John Hightower, first pastor, served until 1813. Meeting house shared with other denominations. Services through Civil War while most did not. The present building erected in 1866. Warren US 31-W, KY 240, 7 mi. E. of Woodburn Markers

documents.title: Hobson House
documents.text: Hobson House Located at the west end of Main St. Home of Col. Atwood G. Hobson, lawyer, banker and Union officer, begun 1860. During the Confederate occupation of Bowling Green, 1862, CSA Gen. Simon B. Buckner saved house at request of his friend, USA General W. E. Hobson, son of owner. Used as munitions depot. After the war, Col. Hobson made that his home until death, 1898. Warren 1100 West Main St., Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: Long Hunters
documents.text: Long Hunters An exploring party of 13 "Long Hunters," so named because of the long periods of time spent away from home, camped along Barren River in 1775. Their names were carved on a beech tree, a silent record of the first white men in this area. Henry Skaggs and Joseph Drake of this group had been among first Long Hunters, 1769-71, whose exploring helped open mid-Kentucky. Warren Courthouse lawn, US 68, 231, Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: Pioneer Surveyor
documents.text: Pioneer Surveyor General Elijah M. Covington of the Kentucky Militia came here from North Carolina in 1795 to farm and survey. Acquired 23,000 acres in Warren, Logan, Edmonson counties. He became Warren County's first sheriff and surveyor. Helped to select the early site of Bowling Green and made the first survey of Mammoth Cave. This park named for him, purchased by city, 1933. Warren Covington Woods Park,US 31-W, Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: Ogden College
documents.text: Ogden College Founded here, 1877, with funds left by Robert Ogden, local businessman. Filled educational gap, as there were no public schools here until 1882. Prep school accredited in 1919. Ogden's criteria: regular attendance, gentlemanly deportment, diligent study. Consolidated with Western Ky. Univ., 1927. Its name is retained in the Ogden College of Science and Technology. Warren State St. at 15th St., Ogden Campus, Western Ky. Univ. Markers

documents.text: Fort Webb Constructed by CSA during early days of Civil War. One of numerous fortifications in Bowling Green area used by CSA and Union forces. Located at head of navigation on Barren and Green River systems, Bowling Green became an important stronghold with two railroads to Memphis and Nashville. Threats from Union forces caused CSA to abandon town on February 14, 1862. Over. documents.text: McFadin's Station First settlement in Warren County, 1/4 mi. east, was on north side of Barren River near mouth of Drake's Creek. Andrew McFadin, Rev. War soldier from N.C., surveyed area and established station, 1785. It was a popular stopover on Cumberland Trace. Emmett Logan, a Louisville Times editor, once owned land where station stood. Henry Watterson was frequent visitor to his home. Warren KY 1402, Porter Pike, Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: Jacob Skiles and Three Springs
documents.text: Jacob Skiles and Three Springs Pioneer merchant Skiles started to Ky. in 1790 by Ohio River flatboat, surviving Indian capture en route. He settled in Bowling Green, 1803, and later moved to Three Springs on the Cumberland Trace. Here he established a thriving mercantile business. Skiles died, 1816. Three Springs declined as an area trade center in 1820s when travel was diverted through Bowling Green. Warren 2055 Three Springs Rd., Bowling Green Markers

documents.title: James T. Morehead, 1797-1854
documents.text: James T. Morehead, 1797-1854 Ky.'s first native son to become governor was born in Bullitt Co. but reared in Logan Co. He read law under John J. Crittenden; began practice in Bowling Green. Served in Ky. House of Rep., and elected lt. gov. At Gov. Breathitt's death, Morehead became chief executive, 1834-1836. A close Whig ally of Henry Clay, he was in U.S. Senate, 1841-1847. Buried in Frankfort. Warren Courthouse, Bowling Green Markers

documents.text: Providence Knob Baptist Church Oldest Missionary Baptist Church in Warren Assoc., it was organized in Sept. 1804 with nine members. Five churches in Bowling Green and Warren Co. have formed from the parent church, including First Baptist Church of Bowling Green, 1818. Two associations formed here: Gasper River-1812; Clear Fork-1860. Present building erected in 1852. Presented by Providence Knob Baptist Church. Warren 210 Browning Road, Jct. documents.title: Jonesville
documents.text: Jonesville This African American community was founded after the Civil War. It was bordered by Dogwood Dr., Russellville Road, and the railroad tracks. The community grew to include several hundred residents, an elementary school, businesses, and two churches. Frame and hand-hewn stone houses lined the streets of Jonesville. Presented by Western Kentucky University. (Reverse) Jonesville - The lives of most residents of this close African American community revolved around church, school and family activities. documents.title: Ora Porter (1880-1970)
documents.text: Ora Porter (1880-1970) Ora Porter, born in Butler Co., in 1880, moved to Bowling Green at age 10. She graduated from Tuskegee Institute School of Nursing and was among the earliest registered nurses in Ky. She was an organizer of the George Washington Carver Community Center, the Interracial Commission, an active campaigner for civic improvement. Died, 1970. Dedicated July 12, 2005. Warren 229 State Street, Bowling Green, KY Markers

documents.title: Shake Rag
documents.text: Shake Rag This African American community was founded in the 1800s. Bordered by the river and High, Ky., and 7th Sts, the area grew to include hundreds of residents, two schools, businesses, and churches. The architecture of Shake Rag shows a growing middle-class community. (Reverse) The lives of residents revolved around church, school, and family activities. The congregation that became State Street Baptist was organized in 1838. State Street School was founded in 1883; the Carver Center began in 1946. The Southern Queen Hotel served black travelers. documents.title: Training School-College High
documents.text: Training School-College High The model training school opened September 17, 1906, on College Street. It offered 4 grades for Western teacher training. In 1911 moved to future site of Cherry Hall. Grades 5-8 added by 1913. Ties to city schools severed & 9th grade added, 1920. Moved to this site, 1925. Graduated 10 in 1st 4-yr. high school class, 1926. (Reverse) Renamed University High in 1966, the school remained open until May 27, 1970. Directors were Sarah Scott, Laura Frazee, Mattie Hatcher, Leon Stephan, W.L. Matthews, C.H. Jaggers, Dero Downing, and James Carpenter. documents.title: Eliza Calvert Hall, 1856-1935
documents.text: Eliza Calvert Hall, 1856-1935 Lida Calvert Obenchain (“Eliza Calvert Hall”), suffragist, press superintendent of Ky. Equal Rights Assn., poet, author. Her most famous story, “Sally Ann’s Experience” (1898), protested women’s inequality. President Roosevelt praised her first collection of stories, Aunt Jane of Kentucky(1907). Over Royalties helped purchase home at 1353 Chestnut St. The Land of Long Ago(1909), To Love and to Cherish (1911) and Clover and Blue Grass (1916) followed. For A Book of Hand-Woven Coverlets (1912), she bought coverlets from wagons of tobacco farmers on Chestnut St. Her books reached at least one million readers. Over. Dedicated March 30, 2008. documents.title: Ernest Hogan
documents.text: Ernest Hogan Born Reuben Crowdus on April 17, 1865 in Bowling Green, Ky. He left home at age 12 to sing in minstrel shows. He became prominent as a songwriter in the 1890s. In 1895, he wrote “La Pas Ma La” & promoted it as first published ragtime song. Many regarded him as the “Father of Ragtime,” a new genre of music, from which many other types of music developed. (Reverse) A pioneer in black entertainment, he was one of the best-known and highest-paid performers of early ragtime era. He starred in major minstrels, vaudeville, and musical comedy. documents.title: Lillian H. South, 1879-1966
documents.text: Lillian H. South, 1879-1966 A native of Warren Co., Ky., she exerted a powerful influence on public health in Ky. South earned her MD in 1904 and returned to Bowling Green to practice medicine, establishing St. Joseph’s Hospital in her family’s home on 12th St. She served as state bacteriologist from 1911-1951. (Reverse) Dr. South earned national acclaim with her research on hookworms, which led to her election as the 1st female VP of the AMA in 1913. In 1922, she began the first lab tech training program in the US. She led the movement to ban the use of the public drinking cup. As early as the 1930s, she championed the use of vaccines. documents.title: T. C. Cherry Elementary
documents.text: T. C. Cherry Elementary Named for Dr. Thomas Crittenden Cherry, who was superintendent of the Bowling Green schools for 32 years (1905-37). T. C. Cherry Elem. began educating children in the fall of 1950. It housed grades K-8, which included the first kindergarten offered by Bowling Green public schools. Cherry Elementary opened on August 8, 2009. “The urge to know is a glorious fever. Fortunate is the youth who has caught it.” -Thomas C. Cherry Dedicated October 17, 2010. documents.title: Presbyterian Church
documents.text: Presbyterian Church Presbyterian Church - Pioneer Cemetery, the earliest public burying ground in Bowling Green, was established in 1811. The Presbyterian Church was later constituted on these grounds on April 9, 1819 by Rev. Joseph B. Lapsley (1779-1823). His remains are interred here at the site of the original pulpit. Worship moved to a new edifice, designed by architect Hugh Roland, in 1837. (Reverse) Presbyterian Church - The Church relocated to State St. and Tenth Ave. in 1833. It was designed for worship and to house a successful female academy. Both operated until the Civil War, when a hospital occupied the structure. documents.title: State Street United Methodist Church
documents.text: State Street United Methodist Church State Street United Methodist Church - Reverend Andrew Monroe, a circuit rider, conducted the first Methodist service in Warren County in 1809 at a local tavern. By 1819, a Methodist Society held meetings at a home on Center Street. In 1820, the first church was constructed and pastored by Reverend Benjamin Moore. In 1842, a larger church was built on State Street. State Street United Methodist Church - In late 1844, the Methodist Church split into northern and southern factions because of slavery. Known as the Methodist Episcopal Church, South from 1844-1939, this church built the current Romanesque- Revival structure in 1895 from Warren Co. limestone. I

documents.title: Washington County
documents.text: Washington County The first county formed by first Assembly of Kentucky, 1792. Named for Geo. Washington. Springfield, county seat, laid off, 1793, by Matthew Walton; veteran of War of Revolution, legislator. Courthouse built in 1816, oldest used as such in state (1965). First settlers in area, 1776. Pres. Lincoln's grandfather came this part Ky., 1782; parents married in county, 1806. Over. (Reverse) Washington Co. Contd. - Col. John Hardin, Revolutionary soldier, laid claim in area, 1780. Settled, 1786. On peace mission in Ohio, 1792, murdered by Indians. First Dominican Priory in U.S., 1806, where Jefferson Davis went to school, 1815-16. documents.title: Felix Grundy (1777-1840)
documents.text: Felix Grundy (1777-1840) Grundy gained prominence in Ky. as a celebrated criminal lawyer and political leader. He practiced law on Main St., Springfield, took part in 2nd Constitutional Conv., served Washington County in legislature (1800-02); Nelson Co. (1804-1806). Became judge to Court of Appeals, then Chief Justice of Ky., in 1807. In U.S. Senate, from Tenn. 1829-38; 1839-40; was U.S. Attorney General, 1838-39. documents.text: Grundy Plantation Settled by George and Elizabeth Grundy in 1780 after fleeing war-torn Berkeley Co., Va.. This wilderness frontier of Va., then called Kaintuckee, became a state in 1792. Son Samuel stayed on the farm and expanded it. Another son Felix chose law and politics. This portion of the farm still remains in the Grundy family. (Reverse) Felix Grundy- Gained prominence as a celebrated criminal lawyer & political leader. documents.title: Lincoln Homestead State Park
documents.text: Lincoln Homestead State Park Thomas and Nancy Hanks Lincoln, the parents of future president Abraham Lincoln, were married near here on June 12, 1806. Shortly after their wedding, the couple moved to Elizabethtown, where their daughter, Sarah, was born. The family eventually lived near Hodgenville, where Abraham Lincoln was born on Feb. 12, 1809. (Reverse) Nancy died of milk sickness in 1818, when Abraham was 9 years old. His father, a farmer and carpenter, died in Ill. in 1851. Mordecai Lincoln, Abraham’s uncle, lived a half-mile south of here. Mordecai also moved to Ill., and, Lincoln wrote, “I often saw Uncle Mordecai.” Lincoln Homestead State Park was established 1936. documents.title: 1917 Coal Mine Explosion
documents.text: 1917 Coal Mine Explosion 1917 Coal Mine Explosion - On Aug. 4, 1917 about 7:40 AM an explosion in the West Kentucky Coal Company’s #7 mine shattered the community of Clay. The worst mine disaster in state history was caused by methane gas and an opened-flame headlamp. At the time of the explosion miners were on strike, protesting low wages and dangerous working conditions. Over. (Reverse) 1917 Coal Mine Explosion - Many miners killed were African Americans from the South, employed as strike breakers. documents.text: Cumberland Falls Moonbow The Moonbow that appears here is the only one in the Western Hemisphere. It may be observed under a full moon and a clear sky. An arch of white light is usually produced at base of Falls and continues downstream. Generations of people have visited here to see this natural phenomenon. Last hotel on this site, Moonbow Inn, was named for the moonbow. Whitley 7351 Hwy. 90, Corbin Markers

documents.title: Morgan at Midway
documents.text: Morgan at Midway Taking 300 abandoned USA horses and mules at Versailles, Morgan's Raiders came here July 15, 1862. Advised of troop train approach from Frankfort he had tracks torn up and howitzers set. Train warned and returned to Frankfort. Morgan took telegraph line and coaxed train at Lexington to come on but it turned back. He and his men reached Georgetown that evening. Woodford US 62 at railroad, Midway Markers

documents.title: Sue Mundy" Here
documents.text: Sue Mundy" Here Jerome Clarke, called Sue Mundy, one of Morgan's Raiders, formed his own guerrilla band on Morgan's death Sept. 1864. Clarke and band raided here November 1, 1864, killing Adam Harper. Four Confederate prisoners executed in reprisal by Union forces. On Feb. 2, 1865, Clarke returned with William Quantrill, another guerrilla leader, burned depot here and stole 15 horses. Woodford US 62, Midway Markers

Opened battle at Mechanicsville; fought at Cedar Mt., 2nd Bull Run, in latter seriously wounded, never fully recovering. 1864, maj. gen. in command Hood's Texas div. Bore heavy part in battles at Cold Harbor and Petersburg. His division half of Lee's army and only effective fighting unit intact left to surrender at Appomattox. Brig. General James S. documents.title: Morgan's First Raid
documents.text: Morgan's First Raid On first Kentucky raid CSA Gen. John H. Morgan with 900 cavalry in Lawrenceburg July 14, 1862; came here that night. Sent out scouts in all directions and took 300 USA horses and mules. Next day moved to Georgetown, then to Cynthiana, after which returned to Tennessee. See map on other side. On raid Morgan covered 1,000 miles in 24 days, raiding 17 towns. Woodford US 60, 62, Versailles Markers

documents.title: Woodford County Hemp
documents.text: Woodford County Hemp One of chief producing counties, crop income reached a yearly high of $125,000 in the 1840s. documents.title: Woodford County, 1789
documents.text: Woodford County, 1789 Last of nine formed by Virginia before Kentucky became a state in 1792. Original county taken from Fayette and extended as far north as the Ohio River; included the area of 7 present counties and parts of 4 others. (Reverse) County Named - For General William Woodford, a Virginian, commander of the First Brigade of the Continental army. Active in campaign to drive out Lord Dunmore, the colonial governor of Virginia, who later left the colonies and returned to England. documents.title: Huntertown
documents.text: Huntertown HUNTERTOWN - Huntertown was an African-American hamlet in Woodford County settled after the Civil War. On August 29, 1871, Jerry Gatewood, who was formerly enslaved and a veteran of the USCT, bought the first 5-acre tract from Isham Railey of the Hunter family to form the Huntertown community. Railey originally purchased the 50-acre site for 34 mules and $5. HUNTERTOWN - For over 130 years, Huntertown was a close-knit community located on what was formerly called Crawfish Pike in Versailles. documents.title: Big Bone Lick
documents.text: Big Bone Lick Big Bone Lick was a mineral spring where Pleistocene mastodons, mammoths, and ground sloths left bones in the mud while seeking salt. Native peoples and later explorers—including Christopher Gist—collected fossils here; Thomas Jefferson later studied specimens from the lick. The site became Big Bone Lick State Historic Site, one of Kentucky’s earliest windows on deep time and a waypoint for salt hunters on the Ohio frontier. Boone History

documents.title: Lexington Named
documents.text: Lexington Named In early June 1775, William McConnell’s surveyors camped on a sinking spring of Elkhorn Creek when word arrived of the April 19 fight at Lexington, Massachusetts. They named the camp for that battle and returned east; permanent settlement waited until 1779, when Robert Patterson’s party built a blockhouse near present Main and Mill. Virginia established the town in 1782—the springs chose the site, the Revolution chose the name. Fayette History

documents.title: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
documents.text: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station In 1775 Benjamin Logan left Boone's party and built Logan's Station (St. Asaph) near present-day Stanford—a stockade by Buffalo Spring that held through a roughly thirteen-day siege in May 1777. Logan hauled the wounded Burr Harrison inside under fire, then slipped out at night and walked about 150 miles to the Holston settlements for powder. He later helped write Kentucky's first constitution and settled on Bullskin Creek near Finchville in Shelby County. Lincoln History

documents.title: Shelbyville Founding
documents.text: Shelbyville Founding Shelby County was carved from Jefferson County in 1792 and named for first governor Isaac Shelby. That October, at the first county court, Revolutionary veteran William Shannon donated about 50 acres on Clear Creek so the new seat would sit on the Frankfort-to-Falls road. Trustees required hewed-log houses with brick or stone chimneys; by 1800 the town had 262 people. Nearby Squire Boone's Painted Stone Station had been the earlier foothold—Shelbyville won the courthouse. Shelby County seat History

documents.title: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
documents.text: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase West of the Tennessee River, Chickasaw hunting grounds stayed off Kentucky's settled map until October 19, 1818. Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby negotiated what became the Jackson Purchase: roughly 13,000 square miles (about 2,369 in Kentucky) for annuities. That treaty filled in the western counties from Ballard through McCracken and closed the last big Indigenous title claim inside the state. Western Kentucky History

documents.title: Frankfort Founding
documents.text: Frankfort Founding Before it was the capital, the site was a buffalo-trail ford on the Kentucky River. In 1780 pioneer Stephen Frank was killed in a skirmish there; settlers called the crossing Frank's Ford, which shortened to Frankfort. In 1786 Virginia chartered a town on land promoted by Gen. James Wilkinson. When Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort outbid rivals for the capital, and Gideon Shryock's Greek Revival Old Capitol (1830) finally stuck after earlier buildings burned. Franklin History

documents.title: Bullitt's Lick Salt Works
documents.text: Bullitt's Lick Salt was frontier white gold, and the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the Revolution sat about three miles west of present-day Shepherdsville. Capt. Thomas Bullitt surveyed the Salt River lick in 1773; production started in 1779 as workers boiled brine in rows of iron kettles. Pack trains and flatboats carried the salt across Kentucky, a fort went up in 1780, and a boomtown nicknamed Saltburg grew around the furnaces until cheaper salt arrived around 1830. Bullitt History

documents.title: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
documents.text: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island Virginia surveyor-turned-militia leader George Rogers Clark staged at Corn Island in the Falls of the Ohio in 1778, then launched the Illinois Campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes from the British. The settlement he left behind became Louisville, chartered in 1780 and named for France’s Louis XVI. Fort Nelson later rose on the mainland as his western headquarters. Jefferson History

documents.title: Battle of Blue Licks
documents.text: Battle of Blue Licks On August 19, 1782, about 182 Kentucky militia chasing Captain William Caldwell’s raiders walked into an ambush on a Licking River ridge in today’s Robertson County. Roughly 50 Butler’s Rangers and 200–300 Shawnee, Delaware, and Wyandot warriors fired from ravines and bluffs; Todd, Trigg, and Boone’s son Israel were among the dead. It was the settlers’ bloodiest Revolutionary defeat in Kentucky, months after Yorktown. Robertson History

documents.title: Great Saltpetre Cave
documents.text: Great Saltpetre Cave South of Mount Vernon in Rockcastle County, Great Saltpetre Cave was mined hard for calcium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades cut off imported saltpeter for gunpowder. Dozens of workers (many enslaved) leached cave earth in wooden vats and shipped crystals to powder mills until trade reopened after 1815. The Rockcastle Karst Conservancy keeps the preserve today. Rockcastle History

documents.title: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
documents.text: Richard Henderson / Transylvania North Carolina judge Richard Henderson reorganized his investors as the Transylvania Company in early 1775, then bargained at Sycamore Shoals for roughly 20 million acres between the Kentucky, Cumberland, and Ohio rivers. Cherokee headmen signed in mid-March; warrior Dragging Canoe opposed the sale and warned the country would become dark and bloody. Virginia later voided the private purchase but compensated the company with Ohio River acreage that seeded Henderson County. Henderson History

documents.title: Bardstown Founding
documents.text: Bardstown Founding The Bardstown area was explored in the mid-1770s and briefly called Salem. In 1780 William Bard surveyed a town on a 1,000-acre grant for his brother David and John Cockey Owings and set aside ground for public buildings. Named seat of new Nelson County in 1784, it was chartered by Virginia as Baird’s Town in 1788 and settled into the name Bardstown—one of Kentucky’s oldest inland towns. Nelson County seat History

documents.title: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
documents.text: John Floyd / Floyd's Station Virginia surveyor John Floyd led a 1774 Fincastle party into Kentucky, staked 2,000 acres on Beargrass Creek, and came back in 1779 to stockade Floyd's Station near today's St. Matthews. Virginia made him a Louisville trustee, Jefferson militia colonel, and in 1783 one of Kentucky's first two judges. On April 8 that year he rode toward Bullitt's Lick in a scarlet coat; a shot from ambush dropped him, and he died two days later at 32. Jefferson History

documents.title: Georgetown / Royal Spring
documents.text: Georgetown / Royal Spring In July 1774 John Floyd claimed a thousand acres around a big Bluegrass spring. John McClelland built a cabin and stockade above it in 1775; an attack on December 29, 1776, killed McClelland, and the station emptied in 1777. Baptist preacher Elijah Craig later laid out Lebanon on the same spring, won a 1784 Virginia charter, and in 1790 renamed the place George Town for Washington. Scott County's seat still drinks from Royal Spring. Scott History

documents.title: Leestown
documents.text: Leestown In 1773 the McAfee company and Hancock Taylor surveyed a buffalo crossing on the Kentucky River about a mile north of today’s Frankfort. Hancock and Willis Lee planted a village on the north bank in 1775, the first Anglo-American settlement north of the river. Raids emptied it in 1777; it returned as a tobacco warehouse and shipping port for hemp, corn, and whiskey, and in 1827 limestone for the Old State House was quarried from the riverbank here. Franklin History

documents.title: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
documents.text: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run Daniel's younger brother Squire Boone carved his name into a Clear Creek rock, painted the letters red, and by spring 1780 planted Shelby County's first large station about two miles north of present Shelbyville. After an April 1781 wound left Squire's right arm permanently short, most settlers fled toward Linn's Station and walked into the Long Run Massacre of September 13. He later rebuilt a mill on the burnt site before land debts cost him the station. Shelby & Jefferson counties History

documents.title: Paris Founding
documents.text: Paris Founding Joseph Houston's 1776 station sat near Doyle Spring. Lawrence Protzman later platted 250 acres and in 1789 got Virginia to charter the town as Hopewell as Bourbon County's seat. In 1790 James Garrard and locals renamed it Paris to match the county, itself named for France's Bourbon kings who backed the Revolution. The post office briefly ran as Bourbonton before Paris stuck. Bourbon County seat History

documents.title: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
documents.text: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters Shawnee held the larger northern and central Kentucky hunting grounds; Cherokee worked closer to Cumberland Gap. When long hunters stacked pelts for eastern markets, Native parties treated them as poachers. Around late 1769 a Shawnee band with Captain Will Emery took Boone and John Stewart’s six-month haul and warned them home: stay out, or the wasps and yellowjackets would sting. Not blank wilderness—a contested commons. Warren History

documents.title: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
documents.text: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company Fifteen-plus years before Boone’s fame, the Ohio Company hired surveyor Christopher Gist to probe the Ohio Valley down toward the Falls. Crossing into Kentucky from the Scioto mouth, his journal logged rich bottomlands, canebrakes, buffalo plains, and Native towns. Shawnee at Lower Shawneetown warned him off the Falls; he brought the company a fossil “beest” tooth from Big Bone country and the first detailed English read of northeastern Kentucky. Fayette History

documents.title: Jacob Spears
documents.text: Jacob Spears Pennsylvania-born Revolutionary veteran Jacob Spears settled near Paris in Bourbon County and was distilling by the 1790s. Thomas Metcalfe built his stone house (“Stone Castle”) around 1790; the farm still holds a springhouse and whiskey storehouse—Kentucky’s most complete early distiller’s complex. Spears floated barrels down the Licking to the Ohio and on to New Orleans, and he is often credited among the first to market the county’s whiskey under the name that stuck: bourbon. Bourbon History

documents.title: John Filson
documents.text: John Filson Pennsylvania schoolteacher and surveyor John Filson reached Lexington around 1783 with land warrants for more than 12,000 acres. In 1784 he published The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke—the first written history of the country—with a companion map engraved in Philadelphia. The book’s appendix carried the earliest printed Boone narrative; in 1788 Filson helped plat Losantiville (later Cincinnati) and that October vanished while surveying near the Great Miami. Jefferson History

documents.title: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
documents.text: Lexington & Ohio Railroad On January 27, 1830, Kentucky chartered the Lexington & Ohio—the commonwealth’s first railroad, and among the first west of the Alleghenies—to tie Lexington to the Ohio River. Track used English strap iron spiked to quarried limestone sills; horses pulled early cars, then steam. The “Daniel Boone” engine made Lexington to Frankfort in about two and a half hours in 1835, cracking open Bluegrass freight toward the river long before the Civil War. Franklin History

documents.title: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
documents.text: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station Born Spotsylvania County, Va., October 16, 1761, Bland Williams Ballard came to Kentucky in 1779 and scouted for George Rogers Clark. With Robert Tyler he helped plant Tyler Station on Tick Creek east of Shelbyville around 1781. In 1788 Delaware warriors killed his father and several siblings near the station; Ballard fought through Fallen Timbers, survived capture at Frenchtown, represented Shelby County in the General Assembly, and died September 5, 1853. Ballard County carries his name. Shelby History

documents.title: Gaitskill Mound
documents.text: Gaitskill Mound On Mount Sterling’s northern bypass, Gaitskill Mound is an Adena earthwork (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 700) listed on the National Register in 1975. Unlike many looted mounds, it yielded rare engraved stone and clay tablets recovered through University of Kentucky work associated with W.S. Webb—ritual objects tied to Adena cremation and mound ceremony rather than everyday trash. The site anchors Montgomery County’s deep Woodland past beneath the later townscape. Montgomery History

documents.title: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
documents.text: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper Scottish physician-chemist James C. Crow began advising Oscar Pepper's Woodford County farm still on Glenn's Creek by 1833. After Pepper rebuilt in stone (1837–38), Crow returned as master distiller (1840–55), measuring mash temperatures, yeast, and acidity with scientific care that fixed sour-mash practice as commercial habit. His whiskey shipped far beyond Kentucky; Old Crow later took his name, and the limestone valley still hosts Woodford Reserve on the old Pepper ground. Woodford History

documents.title: Isaac Shelby
documents.text: Isaac Shelby Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant, then helped lead the Overmountain Men to victory at Kings Mountain in 1780. He moved to Kentucky in the 1780s, helped push statehood, and in 1792 became the commonwealth's first governor; sixteen years later he returned as fifth governor and led militia at the Battle of the Thames. Shelby County still carries his name, and Traveler's Rest marks his home ground. Lincoln History

documents.title: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill
documents.text: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill Near Crab Orchard, William Whitley finished Sportsman's Hill (1787–1794), often called Kentucky's first brick house—thick walls, elevated windows, and hiding places against raids. Beside it he ran a clay oval where horses raced counter-clockwise, a pointed break from English turf clockwise. The house and hill remain a Lincoln County historic site. Lincoln History

documents.title: Estill's Defeat
documents.text: Estill's Defeat On March 22, 1782, Capt. James Estill and about 25 Lincoln County militiamen overtook a Wyandot raiding party at Little Mountain Creek, near today’s Mount Sterling. After nearly two hours of fighting, Lt. William Miller’s left flank broke, the Wyandots closed, and Estill was killed in hand-to-hand combat along with six of his men. The fight—also called the Battle of Little Mountain—was one of the bloodiest single engagements of Kentucky’s “Year of Blood.” Montgomery History

documents.title: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
documents.text: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker In March 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker led a Loyal Land Company party through the Appalachians and on April 13 recorded Cave Gap: a plain Indian road, a spring pouring from a cave, marked trees, and a pass visible for miles. He named the gap and nearby river for the Duke of Cumberland and later had a small cabin raised near present Barbourville—the first Euro-American house claimed in Kentucky. Walker’s journal mapped the geologic doorway later generations would pour through. Bell History

documents.title: Catherine Spears Carpenter
documents.text: Catherine Spears Carpenter Twice-widowed Catherine Spears Carpenter ran a large Casey County farm after 1806, raising crops, livestock, and surplus corn into whiskey. County tax records show her paying on 100 gallons of spirits in 1815. An 1818 manuscript in the Carpenter Family Papers preserves sweet-mash and sour-mash distilling recipes she used to instruct her household—one of the earliest written American sour-mash records, decades before James Crow’s fame. Casey History

documents.title: Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site
documents.text: Wickliffe Mounds Mississippian farmers founded Wickliffe around AD 1100 on a bluff over the Ohio, three miles from the Mississippi confluence. They built platform mounds, a plaza, houses, and after 1175 a cemetery mound; by 1350 the community capped its mounds and left. In the 1930s a promoter opened graves to tourists as “Ancient Buried City”; Murray State later professionalized the research, and the site became a state historic site in 2004. Ballard History

documents.title: Falls of the Ohio
documents.text: Falls of the Ohio About 390 million years ago a shallow Devonian sea laid down the Jeffersonville Limestone—coral banks and stromatoporoid sponges now exposed at the Falls of the Ohio. Those hard shelves made the only major rapids on the river, so flatboats had to portage; Louisville and the Indiana towns grew at that choke point. George Rogers Clark staged from Corn Island in 1778. The beds have been a National Natural Landmark since 1966. Clarksville History

documents.title: Lower Shawneetown
documents.text: Lower Shawneetown Long before stations dotted the Bluegrass, a major Shawnee town straddled the Ohio at the Scioto’s mouth near today’s South Portsmouth. English maps called it Lower Shawneetown; by 1751 eyewitnesses put the population around 1,200. It was a diplomatic hub and western end of Pennsylvania’s southern deerskin trade until 1758, when the Shawnee moved north. Kentucky archaeology still holds Fort Ancient pottery mixed with mid-1700s trade goods from the Bentley and related sites on the Kentucky bank. Greenup History

documents.title: Indian Knoll
documents.text: Indian Knoll Five thousand years before the first stations, Late Archaic hunter-gatherers kept returning to a shell midden on the Green River in Ohio County. Indian Knoll (15OH2) yielded over a thousand burials, twenty-three dog burials, and more than 50,000 artifacts when University of Kentucky crews dug it in the late 1930s WPA years. In the early 1990s it and nineteen other Green River shell middens became National Historic Landmarks. History

documents.title: Danville Constitution Square
documents.text: Danville Constitution Square After the Kentucky District court moved from Harrodsburg to Crow’s Station, Danville’s public square (laid out 1785) hosted ten conventions from 1784 to 1792. Delegates there framed the first state constitution in April 1792, clearing the way for Kentucky to enter the Union as the fifteenth state on June 1. Replicas of the log courthouse, jail, and meetinghouse still mark the ground. Boyle History

documents.title: Mount Horeb Adena / Adena Park
documents.text: Mount Horeb Adena / Adena Park Above Elkhorn Creek near Lexington, Adena people built a circular ditch-and-embankment enclosure more than 2,000 years ago for periodic ritual gatherings. WPA digs under William S. Webb in 1939 found a ring of large paired posts that likely screened ceremonies before the earthen walls went up. The University of Kentucky now protects a partially reconstructed site as Adena Park. Fayette History

documents.title: Fox Farm Fort Ancient
documents.text: Fox Farm Fort Ancient On a broad ridgetop near Mays Lick, Fort Ancient farmers lived at Fox Farm (15Ms1) from about 1300 into the mid-1600s—one of the longest-lived villages of its kind in the Ohio Valley. Houses first ringed a plaza, then clustered around a large public building as population grew. Residents planted corn, beans, and squash, managed turkey harvests, and once curated eleven deer jaws as a ritual offering inside a house wall. Mason History

documents.title: Indian Fort Mountain
documents.text: Indian Fort Mountain On a knobby ridge south of Berea, dry-laid stone walls ring Indian Fort Mountain (15Ma25) in the Berea College Forest. Hopewell-era Middle Woodland people built them about 2,000 years ago as a hilltop enclosure, more a ceremonial marker than a stockade. Tests in 1980 treated the tumbled rock as linear mounds rather than a fighting wall. The site went on the National Register in 1983; hikers still climb the Pinnacles over the same ground. Madison History

documents.title: Ashland Central Park Adena Mounds
documents.text: Ashland Central Park Adena Mounds Six conical Adena burial mounds still sit in Ashland’s Central Park, roughly 15–20 feet across and 4–6 feet high in a slight curve. UK archaeologists Webb and Funkhouser recorded them in 1932; a 1930s survey said no Kentucky city held more prehistoric evidence than Ashland, though many other local mounds were leveled for streets. Listed on the National Register in 1974, they mark Woodland mound-builder presence along the Ohio centuries before historic tribes. Boyd History

documents.title: Mount Sterling Founding
documents.text: Mount Sterling Founding Explorers out of Boonesborough called a tree-covered Adena burial mound “the Little Mountain.” Scotsman Hugh Forbes began selling lots beside it around 1790; in 1792 the Kentucky Assembly chartered the town on 640 acres. Forbes meant Mount Stirling (for Stirling, Scotland, plus the mound); the misspelled “Sterling” stuck. The mound—once about 25 feet high at Queen and Locust—was leveled in 1845, and Mount Sterling became Montgomery County’s seat. Montgomery County seat History

documents.title: Carlston Annis Shell Mound
documents.text: Carlston Annis Shell Mound On the Green River floodplain in Butler County, Carlston Annis (15Bt5) is a Late Archaic shell midden about 300 by 350 feet and more than six feet thick, piled up beside a mussel shoal between roughly 3000 and 1000 BC. WPA crews under William S. Webb dug nearly half an acre in 1940–41; later work by the Shell Mound Archaeological Project refined the picture of repeated seasonal camps with burials, dog burials, hearths, and pestle caches. Butler History
