documents.title: Winchester Founding
documents.text: Winchester Founding Clark County was carved from Fayette and Bourbon on December 6, 1792, and named for George Rogers Clark. Justices first met at John Strode’s station, then voted to put the public buildings on John Baker’s land by his spring. On December 17, 1793, the Assembly established a town there named Winchester, after Baker’s hometown in Frederick County, Virginia. A two-room log courthouse went up in 1794; Winchester remains Clark’s seat. History

documents.title: Hardin Village Fort Ancient
documents.text: Hardin Village Fort Ancient On the Ohio floodplain in Greenup County near South Shore, Hardin Village was a late Fort Ancient town occupied from the late 1500s into the early 1600s and covering more than ten acres. University of Kentucky digs in 1939 and again in the 2010s mapped large bark-walled houses, storage pits, and family cemeteries. Triangular endscrapers point to intensive hide work for long-distance exchange—marine shell and brass among the imports—just as the protohistoric Ohio Valley was tipping toward abandonment. Greenup History

documents.title: Richmond Founding
documents.text: Richmond Founding Madison County's first seat sat at hillside Milford with thin water. In 1798 the legislature let the court move onto Revolutionary War veteran Col. John Miller's land along Otter Creek; the county paid angry Milford residents before carting records to Miller's barn. On July 4, 1798, trustees named the new seat Richmond for Miller's Virginia birthplace, surveyed fifty acres into lots, and built a brick courthouse on the barn site in 1799. Richmond incorporated in 1809. Madison History

documents.text: Wright Mounds (Montgomery County Adena) Three conical Adena mounds (15Mm6–8) once crowned a Bluegrass ridgetop in Montgomery County. documents.title: Stanford / St. Asaph (Logan’s Fort)
documents.text: Stanford / St. Asaph (Logan’s Fort) In spring 1775 Benjamin Logan and John Floyd’s survey party camped at Buffalo Spring and planted St. Asaph; Logan’s Fort rose there by early 1777 and never fell—nicknamed Standing Fort after the May 1777 siege. On May 16, 1786, the court seated permanently on Logan’s fifty-acre gift a mile east as Stanford, still Lincoln County’s seat. History

Later readings also treat the fiber, cradleboard, and medicinal plants as a possible women’s retreat and medicine place. History

documents.title: Col. John Todd of Lexington
documents.text: Col. John Todd of Lexington Pennsylvania-born lawyer John Todd (1750–1782) reached Kentucky around 1775, sat in Virginia’s legislature for Kentucky County, rode with George Rogers Clark to Kaskaskia and Vincennes, and was named civil commandant of Illinois County. He became Fayette’s first militia colonel and a Lexington trustee. After Bryan Station’s siege he led the pursuit that ended at Blue Licks on August 19, 1782, where he was killed at 32; Todd County (1819) still carries his name. History

documents.text: Muir Site (15Js86) West of Nicholasville on a Jessamine County ridge, Muir is an early Fort Ancient (Osborne phase) hamlet dated roughly A.D. 1000–1200. UK crews dug it in 1985 ahead of the Nicholasville Bypass and found only one to three small square-to-rectangular basin houses in use at a time—dispersed households rather than a later plaza village. Muir shows Bluegrass Fort Ancient life before the big nucleated towns. History

He named it for Admiral Christopher Newport of Jamestown fame, reserved a public square and riverfront common, and in 1803 sold the army five acres at the Licking mouth for what became Newport Barracks. Platform mounds around a central plaza (plus a smaller plaza southwest), deep village middens, and occupation roughly 1100–1500 CE place it with sister border towns like Wickliffe and Sassafras Ridge. documents.title: Maj. Joseph Bowman
documents.text: Maj. Joseph Bowman Virginia-born Joseph Bowman came to Kentucky by 1775, signed the 1776 Harrodsburg county petition, and in 1778 raised a company for George Rogers Clark. As Clark’s second-in-command he took Prairie du Rocher, St. Philippe, and Cahokia after Kaskaskia fell, kept a day-by-day journal of the flooded winter march to Vincennes, and was promoted major just as a celebratory powder explosion burned him badly. He died at Fort Patrick Henry on about August 14–15, 1779 — the only American officer lost in the Illinois campaign. History

His son David Snowden Jr. (1786–1852) built a log cabin, kitchen, and quarters here about 1825; a later two-story clapboard house on sandstone had a wing that served as the St. Helens post office. documents.text: Ashland Iron & Steel / Armco Works Area Ashland’s riverfront iron and steel works grew from Hanging Rock charcoal furnaces into modern steelmaking under Norton Iron Works and later Armco. documents.title: Churchill Weavers (historic)
documents.text: Churchill Weavers (historic) Founded in 1922 by David Carroll and Eleanor Churchill, Churchill Weavers became one of America’s best-known handweaving manufactories and a cornerstone of Berea’s craft industry. The historic weaving operation helped define Berea as a national craft center; related buildings remain part of the town’s manufacturing heritage. documents.title: Ford Louisville Assembly Plant
documents.text: Ford Louisville Assembly Plant Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant on Fern Valley Road has been a cornerstone of Kentucky automotive manufacturing since the mid-twentieth century. Together with the nearby Kentucky Truck Plant, it represents Louisville’s rise as a mass auto-production center after the brief 1909–10 Lexington Motor Car Company experiment. documents.title: Lexington Motor Car Company (plant site)
documents.text: Lexington Motor Car Company (plant site) Lexington Motor Car Company (also called Lexington Motor Company) assembled automobiles here beginning March 1909 under promoter Kinzea Stone, on a rail-served lot west of Calvary Cemetery across from Lexington Cemetery. The firm relocated to Connersville, Indiana in 1910; the Kentucky plant site is now occupied by Palumbo Lumber—correct historic Lexington auto works (not LexTran). documents.text: Louisville Cotton Mill First cotton mill in Louisville (1889), a major Victorian industrial complex that first made cotton warp for “Kentucky Jeans.” Later Louisville Textile Co. / Fincastle Fabrics sold worldwide; by 1948 Louisville Textiles was Kentucky’s largest textile employer. documents.text: Goose Creek Salt Works Strategic Civil War–era salt works on Goose Creek. documents.title: Barren River Lake State Resort Park
documents.text: Barren River Lake State Resort Park Resort park on the north shore of Barren River Lake in south-central Kentucky. The lodge, cottages, and marina anchor boating, fishing, and golf on one of the region’s major Corps lakes. Visitors use it as a base for lake recreation and nearby Mammoth Cave country drives. documents.title: Big Bone Lick State Historic Site
documents.text: Big Bone Lick State Historic Site Called the birthplace of American vertebrate paleontology for Ice Age bones found at its salt lick. Trails, a museum, and outdoor bison herd interpret prehistoric and frontier natural history. Northern Kentucky visitors reach it about 30–40 minutes south of Cincinnati. Union Boone Parks

documents.title: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
documents.text: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park Marks the August 1782 Battle of Blue Licks, often called the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky. Salt springs once drew bison, Native hunters, and pioneers; today a museum, battlefield trail, and lodge interpret that frontier story. The park pairs history with camping and short nature walks. documents.title: Breaks Interstate Park
documents.text: Breaks Interstate Park Joint Kentucky–Virginia park protecting the “Grand Canyon of the South,” a deep gorge of the Russell Fork. Lodge lodging, overlooks, and river trails draw visitors to the Pike County–Buchanan County border. Though administered under an interstate compact, it is commonly listed with Kentucky’s resort parks. Elkhorn City Pike Parks

documents.title: Buckhorn Lake State Resort Park
documents.text: Buckhorn Lake State Resort Park Quiet mountain resort on Buckhorn Lake in the eastern Kentucky coalfields. Lodge rooms and cottages overlook a forested Corps reservoir popular for fishing and pontoon boating. The park is a low-key base for exploring Perry County and nearby Daniel Boone National Forest roads. Buckhorn Perry Parks

documents.text: Carr Creek State Park Recreation park on Carr Creek Lake in Knott County. Camping, a beach, and boat ramps serve eastern Kentucky lake weekends. The setting is classic Appalachian ridge-and-hollow country around a Corps reservoir. Sassafras Knott Parks

documents.title: Carter Caves State Resort Park
documents.text: Carter Caves State Resort Park Cave-and-ridge park in northeastern Kentucky with guided tours of Cascade and X Cave and miles of surface trails. Lodge and cottages sit among wooded karst country near the Ohio River hills. Equestrian camping and a small lake round out a classic Kentucky resort-park stay. Olive Hill Carter Parks

documents.title: Columbus-Belmont State Park
documents.text: Columbus-Belmont State Park Civil War bluff park overlooking the Mississippi River at Columbus. Confederate fortifications, a massive anchor-and-chain display, and museum exhibits interpret the 1861–62 river war. Picnic areas and overlooks make it a western Kentucky history stop. documents.title: Cumberland Falls State Resort Park
documents.text: Cumberland Falls State Resort Park Home of Cumberland Falls—the “Niagara of the South”—and one of the few places in the Western Hemisphere where a moonbow can appear under a full moon. Historic DuPont Lodge and Riverview Restaurant overlook the Cumberland River gorge (lodge dining closed for renovations as of late 2025–2026). Trails, cabins, and falls overlooks remain signature park experiences. Corbin Whitley Parks

documents.title: Dale Hollow Lake State Resort Park
documents.text: Dale Hollow Lake State Resort Park Kentucky’s resort foothold on vast Dale Hollow Lake along the Tennessee border. Clear water, smallmouth bass fishing, and marina access draw boaters to the lodge and cottages. Island View Restaurant’s glass walls look out over the lake and forested shoreline. documents.title: Dawkins Line Rail Trail
documents.text: Dawkins Line Rail Trail Multi-use rail-trail on the former Dawkins Line through Johnson and Magoffin counties in eastern Kentucky. Hikers, cyclists, and equestrians follow converted railroad grade through Appalachian countryside. Trailheads and segments remain part of the Kentucky State Parks recreation inventory. Hagerhill Johnson Parks

documents.text: Dr. Thomas Walker State Historic Site Replica of the cabin associated with Dr. Thomas Walker, who explored Kentucky through Cumberland Gap in 1750. Picnic grounds and a short interpretive stop sit near Barbourville. The site honors one of the earliest documented English explorations of the region. Barbourville Knox Parks

documents.text: Fort Boonesborough State Park Living-history fort on the Kentucky River at the site of Daniel Boone’s 1775 settlement. documents.text: General Butler State Resort Park Hilltop resort where the Kentucky River meets the Ohio near Carrollton. Named for Gen. William Orlando Butler, the park mixes lodge lodging, a ski slope in season, and the Butler-Turpin historic house. Two Rivers Restaurant serves park guests overlooking the river confluence country. documents.text: Greenbo Lake State Resort Park Wooded resort on Greenbo Lake in northeastern Kentucky near the Ohio River. Michael Tygart Lodge and Angler's Cove dining cater to anglers and hikers using the park’s trails and lake. The setting is a quiet contrast to the industrial Ohio River corridor nearby. documents.text: Isaac Shelby Cemetery State Historic Site Final resting place of Isaac Shelby, Kentucky’s first and fifth governor and a Revolutionary War leader. documents.title: Jefferson Davis State Historic Site
documents.text: Jefferson Davis State Historic Site Obelisk and visitor center at the birthplace of Jefferson Davis in Fairview. The 351-foot concrete monument dominates the Todd County landscape and interprets Davis’s Kentucky origins. The site is a major Civil War–era landmark on the western Kentucky driving circuit. documents.text: Jenny Wiley State Resort Park Mountain resort on Dewey Lake named for frontier captive Jenny Wiley. May Lodge overlooks pines and water; Music Highway Grill and Dewey’s Lounge serve lodge guests and day visitors. Elk-viewing tours, amphitheater shows, and hiking make it a flagship eastern Kentucky park. Prestonsburg Floyd Parks

documents.text: John James Audubon State Park Museum and nature park in Henderson honoring artist-naturalist John James Audubon, who lived and worked here. documents.text: Natural Bridge State Resort Park Centered on a 65-foot-high sandstone arch and trail network at the edge of the Red River Gorge. Hemlock Lodge and Sandstone Arches Restaurant overlook wooded cliffs; a seasonal skylift shortens the climb to the bridge. documents.text: Pennyrile Forest State Resort Park Resort tucked inside Pennyrile State Forest in western Kentucky. Platform mounds… Near Hickman in Fulton County, on Bayou de Chien toward the Mississippi, the Adams Site is a Mississippian town built over an earlier Late Woodland village. Platform mounds around a central plaza (plus a smaller plaza southwest), deep village middens up to about 1–1.5 meters thick, and occupation roughly 1100–1500 CE place it with sister border towns like Wickliffe and Sassafras Ridge. documents.text: Isaac Shelby, "Old Kings Mountain" Shelby County's namesake was already a frontier celebrity before Kentucky was a state. Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore's War, then helped… Shelby County's namesake was already a frontier celebrity before Kentucky was a state. Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore's War, then helped lead the Overmountain Men to victory at Kings Mountain in 1780, a blow that cracked British control in the South. He moved to Kentucky in the 1780s, helped push statehood, and in 1792 the electoral college unanimously made him the commonwealth's first governor. documents.title: Yuchi on the Green River maps
documents.text: Yuchi on the Green River maps John R. Swanton's federal tribal handbook notes that early colonial maps place a Yuchi (Euchee) town on a Kentucky river matching the Green. The Yuchi were a language-isolate… John R. Swanton's federal tribal handbook notes that early colonial maps place a Yuchi (Euchee) town on a Kentucky river matching the Green. The Yuchi were a language-isolate people of the southern Appalachians and Tennessee Valley who used the Ohio country more as hunting range than permanent farm country; the Green River map mark is one of the few named Yuchi footprints inside present Kentucky, alongside Cherokee claims on the upper Cumberland and Chickasaw claims in the far west.
